analysis.one_liner: Treats companies that move their headquarters abroad to cut their US tax bill as American companies for tax purposes.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 10 Democratic cosponsors in May 2021, never received a committee vote and died in the House Ways and Means Committee when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the tax rules so that a US company that merges with a foreign company and moves its legal headquarters overseas to pay lower taxes is still taxed as an American company. It would apply this test to deals made after May 8, 2014, and to companies where most executives or business activity stay in the United States. The bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote in the Ways and Means Committee and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.who_benefits: US taxpayers benefit because corporations that stop paying US taxes by moving their headquarters on paper would instead keep paying, easing the pressure on individual taxpayers to make up the difference. US-based workers and competing companies benefit because the bill removes the tax advantage rivals gain by relocating headquarters abroad while keeping most operations and management in the United States [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Treats a foreign company that acquires a US company as still subject to US taxation when former US shareholders own more than half the combined firm, or when management and control stay primarily in the United States and the group has significant domestic business activity
Applies the rule retroactively to deals completed after May 8, 2014, covering inversions that have already taken place

Counters the practice of corporate inversions, in which a US company acquires or is acquired by a foreign company and reincorporates in a lower-tax country while keeping most operations, employees, and management in the US
Preserves an exception for companies with substantial genuine business activity in the foreign country where they are organized, so true foreign combinations are not caught

analysis.who_pays: US-based multinational corporations that would relocate their legal headquarters abroad to lower their tax bill, and the tax advisory firms that arrange such deals, would pay US taxes they currently avoid. Consumers might indirectly feel some of that cost if companies pass higher taxes on through prices, though inversions are largely paper relocations.

drawbacks.text: The bill applies retroactively to acquisitions completed after May 8, 2014 — roughly seven years before it was introduced — which would upend the tax treatment of mergers companies completed years earlier under the rules then in force
The more-than-50-percent ownership test would also catch some ordinary cross-border mergers where US shareholders end up with a majority stake, not just deals motivated by taxes

The bill leaves the existing substantial-business-activities exception largely intact and lets the Treasury set the thresholds by regulation, which gives the executive branch considerable discretion over which deals are actually caught

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Stopping paper headquarters moves would keep tax revenue in the US and remove an unfair advantage over companies that stay put, which serves ordinary taxpayers. The main costs are fairness questions from the seven-year retroactive date and the risk that the 50 percent ownership test sweeps in some mergers that are not tax-driven. Those are design flaws an honest supporter would acknowledge, not reasons the goal is wrong; the larger unanswered question is whether Congress will act on inversions at all, and here it did not.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Ways and Means Committee for the rest of the two-year Congress and never got a hearing, a markup, or any vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 4, 2021, and referred the same day to the House Ways and Means Committee
Ten Democratic cosponsors joined the sponsor; no Republican cosponsors are listed
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote appears in the action history; the bill's last recorded action is the referral
The bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Multinationals that relocate their headquarters abroad to cut their US tax bill are better off, because the rule that would have taxed them as domestic companies never advanced. Tax advisory firms that structure such deals also keep the status quo.

for.name: Lloyd Doggett
for.role: U.S. Representative, Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and rallied 10 Democratic cosponsors

against.name: Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred to the Ways and Means Committee, which held no markup and produced no vote on the bill during the Congress

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was entirely Democratic — 10 of 213 House Democrats cosponsored — and the bill never drew Republican support or floor action before the Congress ended.

industries.industry: US multinationals relocating headquarters abroad (corporate inverters)
industries.note: These companies structure mergers so the combined firm is legally foreign while most business stays in the US, cutting their US tax bill. The bill would remove that option by treating them as domestic corporations, so the revenue they would pay is revenue other taxpayers otherwise cover.
Law and accounting firms design and execute inversion transactions. Narrowing the definition of an inversion would reduce demand for that work.

industries.industry: US-headquartered companies competing against inverted rivals
industries.note: The bill tightens the anti-inversion rules but leaves in place the exception for groups with substantial real business activities in the country they reincorporate in, so companies with genuine foreign operations keep their tax treatment.
